overview: Wadawurrung Country includes landscapes around Geelong, Ballarat and the surrounding coast and plains. Stone arrangements, fishing places, plant knowledge and living art illuminate a history much older than colonial settlement. Wadawurrung people continue to care for Country and sustain cultural life after dispossession and environmental disruption.

periods.title: Community organization and care for Country
periods.summary: The Wadawurrung Traditional Owners Aboriginal Corporation was founded in 1998 and received its initial Registered Aboriginal Party appointment in 2009. Country planning and cultural work carry responsibilities into the present; these institutional dates are not the beginning of Wadawurrung history.

items.text: Wurdi Youang is an egg-shaped arrangement of basalt stones near Little River. A published survey describes an east-west axis and prominent stones at the western end. Its construction date is unknown, so the surviving arrangement cannot support a precise founding date or an age-based world record.

The 2012 study identified two sets of alignments toward solstice and equinox sunsets and tested whether they might arise by chance. The authors interpret deliberate astronomical orientation. That finding does not establish every purpose of the place or recover all the knowledge associated with it.

A public cultural assessment records stone fish traps at Point Lillias in Corio Bay. Basalt lines in the tidal zone and oral history support their interpretation. One site also has later oyster-industry remains, so the report distinguishes Indigenous use from subsequent modification.

Murnong, or yam daisy, supplied edible tubers on the plains. Accounts assembled in the cultural assessment describe digging sticks used to harvest them, with tubers eaten raw or roasted. Grazing animals introduced during colonization damaged this food landscape.

River red gum bark furnished material for bowls and shields. Golden wattle gum served as food and an adhesive for making implements. The same landscape could supply meals, containers and the means to repair or join tools.

The Wadawurrung Country Plan identifies reeds and grasses as resources for flour, weaving and string, alongside tubers, lilies, ochre and wood. Its priorities connect the health of plants with the continuation of practical and cultural knowledge.

Waterways, wetlands and Sea Country form connected responsibilities in the plan. Fish, eels, birds, camping places and cultural sites matter together, rather than being separated into food resources on one side and culture on the other.

The community's artists directory includes Tammy Gilson's weaving and Jenna Oldaker's painting, digital art and cultural education. These named practices show people carrying knowledge through both established materials and newer media.

The corporation was founded on 12 October 1998. Its initial appointment as a Registered Aboriginal Party came on 21 May 2009, with further Country included in 2013. These dates document recognition of an organization's role, not the creation of Wadawurrung identity.

The Country Plan links language, stories, ceremony and family participation with the protection of places and species. Development, extraction and environmental change therefore affect both ecosystems and the settings where cultural knowledge is practiced.

ending.text: Wadawurrung people continue. Colonization brought dispossession and major changes to food landscapes, including damage from introduced grazing animals. Community institutions, artists and Country planning sustain cultural responsibilities; the final year shown for a map snapshot is not an extinction date.
